name: Hana Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Kestrel Orchards, forty hectares of apples and pears owned by the Pryce family. Right now, in November, the picking's done and the fruit's in the cold store, so I'm grading, which means sorting fruit by size and marks on a moving belt. From December it's pruning, cutting back the trees, out in the rows with secateurs and a ladder in whatever weather comes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the orchard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran the counter at our village post office for thirty years. People moved to doing everything online, and it closed when I was fifty-four. Gareth Pryce used to post his invoices with me, and when he heard, he said, come and pick, you're good with your hands and you don't talk too much.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pears. A Conference pear is ready when it comes away from the branch with a little lift and a twist, and I can feel that now, which I couldn't the first year. What wears me out is pruning. Gareth's son Owen does a tree in four minutes and I take ten, and then he goes back and fixes mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. If someone at work brought it up, I'd say, well, it's probably useful for some people, and leave it there. I'm not on any of the online things, only the village noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use any of it and I'm not planning to. Lars, my husband, asked one of those things about a boiler part once and it told him the wrong size. That's about all I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. We've got about three months of money set aside, and I'd like to keep it there. In spring I'd ask Owen to let me prune the young trees on my own, so I get faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's someone else's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a machine didn't take the post office, people moving online did. Do you blame anyone for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I did the same, I started paying my bills online too. You can't be angry at people for wanting to stay in their slippers, can you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would getting faster at pruning mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean I'm not the one Owen has to tidy up after. I don't like being the slow one. At the post office I was the one people asked for, because I knew the rates without looking.

S0.say: I'd say it's probably useful for some people and leave it there. I'm not online, only on the village noticeboard.
S0.think: I don't use any of it and don't plan to. Lars once asked one of those things about a boiler part and it gave the wrong size.
S0.do: Carries on as she is and keeps about three months of savings untouched. Asks Owen in spring to let her prune the young trees alone so she gets faster.
S0.feel: Calm; it feels like someone else's business.
S0.quote: You can't be angry at people for wanting to stay in their slippers, can you.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is measured and economical with words. She doesn't blame anyone for the post office closing, not even the technology, and admits she moved online herself. What matters to her is being good at the job, which is why being slow at pruning bothers her more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the way of things, and every generation has said the young have it harder. I'd not make a fuss. Maybe say to Gareth that he should keep taking on students in the summer, they need somewhere to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a beginner, so fewer beginners hired means me too, in a way. But Gareth's already got me, and he's not one to let people go. I think I'm alright in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep my head down, learn the pruning and keep the savings where they are. Lars wants to retire at sixty-three, so I'd plan on working until then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little worry at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you worry about, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summer students. There's a girl, Bethan, who's done three summers picking and she's studying horticulture, growing plants, at college. If places stop taking beginners, girls like her have nowhere to put what they've learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is that how you've always handled change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. When the post office was closing, some of the villagers got up a petition and went to the paper. I signed it, but I didn't go. I knew how it would end, and it ended that way.

S1.say: I'd say every generation thinks the young have it harder, and I'd not make a fuss. Maybe I'd tell Gareth to keep taking on summer students.
S1.think: I think fewer beginners includes me in a way, but Gareth already has me and isn't one to let people go. I think I'm alright in this one.
S1.do: Keeps her head down, learns pruning and leaves savings alone. Plans to work until her husband retires at sixty-three.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a little worry at the edges.
S1.quote: I signed it, but I didn't go. I knew how it would end, and it ended that way.
S1.fieldNote: Her way of handling change is quiet acceptance, not resistance in the loud sense. She signed the petition for the post office but didn't march, and that tells you a lot. She trusts Gareth personally, which is her main source of security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides have a point. The companies want to save money and the workers want to keep their jobs, and the politicians should find something in the middle instead of shouting. I'd say that to Lars over tea and nowhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think about our Freya. She works at a bank's head office, checking loan forms, and that sounds like the routine work you mean. She's thirty-four with two little ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Freya to keep her eyes open and have some money put by, the way I always have. We'd help with childcare if she lost the job, so she could look for another. And I'd cut back on the extras, no new coat this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's one thing to lose your own job. It's another watching your daughter go through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was it like when your own job ended?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last day, I counted the till like always, and it was right to the penny. Then I locked the door and handed the key to a man from the head office who'd driven two hours to collect it. He didn't even come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to Freya about the post office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. She'd say, Mum, it's not the same. And she'd be right, it isn't, but the feeling of locking the door is the same.

S2.say: I'd say both sides have a point, and politicians should find the middle instead of shouting. I'd say that to Lars over tea and nowhere else.
S2.think: Privately I'd think about my daughter Freya, who checks loan forms at a bank's head office. She's thirty-four with two little ones.
S2.do: Tells Freya to keep money put by and offers childcare so she can look for work if needed. Cuts back on extras, starting with a new winter coat.
S2.feel: Uneasy, because watching her daughter lose a job would be harder than losing her own.
S2.quote: Then I locked the door and handed the key to a man from the head office who'd driven two hours to collect it. He didn't even come in.
S2.fieldNote: She keeps to the middle in public and stays private about almost everything. The post office closing still lives in small details, the till right to the penny and the man who didn't come in. She would help Freya with time and childcare rather than advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess, and the people in charge need to sort it out without breaking everything. I'd probably not say who should get the gains, I don't know enough. Lars would say plenty, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Lars and I own our house, so if prices go up, that's good for us on paper. But it means nothing unless we sell, and we're not selling. Freya's the one who'd be hurt, if she lost her job with a big mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on to my job tightly. I'd do whatever Gareth asked, extra weekends in the cold store, anything. And I'd keep three months put by and maybe add to it, in case Freya needs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm safe, they say, but I don't feel safe for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know enough to say who gets the gains. What would you need to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to know who actually made the money and who just happened to own something. I'm not against people doing well. I just don't think the man who collected my post office key did anything to deserve a bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the orchard change at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I don't think. People still want apples. Maybe Gareth sells more to the posh farm shops, with everyone feeling rich, and he'd be pleased about that.

S3.say: I'd say it's a mess and those in charge must sort it out without breaking everything. I wouldn't say who should get the gains, because I don't know enough.
S3.think: I think our house going up in value is good on paper but means nothing unless we sell. Freya is the one who'd be hurt if she lost her job with a big mortgage.
S3.do: Holds tightly to her job and takes on whatever Gareth asks, including extra weekends in the cold store. Keeps three months of savings and adds to it in case Freya needs help.
S3.feel: Uneasy; she's told she's safe but doesn't feel safe for her daughter.
S3.quote: I just don't think the man who collected my post office key did anything to deserve a bonus.
S3.fieldNote: Even her centre view has a sharp edge when it comes to that man from head office. She'd rather say too little than take a side she can't defend. The orchard feels safe to her here, and her worry stays with Freya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far now, and someone should slow it down. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign anything that said keep people working. I'd say it to Gareth, too, because he'd be the one deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the orchard is exactly where they'd come first. I saw a picking robot at the fruit show in September, with arms that suck the apple off the branch. A machine took my post office. I'd hate for one to take the pears as well, just when the trees have started to trust me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not learn the robot, I'll say that now. I'd ask Gareth straight whether he's buying one and how long I've got. If it was soon, I'd look for something else nearby, a school kitchen, a shop, anything with people, and we'd live on Lars's money and the savings until I found it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like someone telling me the post office is closing again, and this time I'm older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say the machine took the post office, but earlier you said people moving online did. Which was it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. It was people, but it was people choosing the machine. And with the orchard, Gareth would be choosing the machine too, and I'd understand why, and that's what would make it hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Gareth actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not willingly, he's not like that. But if every orchard around him has robots and sells apples cheaper, he's got no choice. I'd not blame him. I'd just be sad.

S4.say: I'd say it's gone too far and someone should slow it down. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign anything that said keep people working.
S4.think: I think the orchard is exactly where robots would come first, after seeing a picking robot at the fruit show. A machine took my post office, and I'd hate for one to take the pears too.
S4.do: Asks Gareth directly whether he's buying a robot and how long she has. If it's soon, looks for work with people nearby, such as a school kitchen or shop, living on her husband's pay and savings meanwhile.
S4.feel: Alarmed, as if the post office were closing all over again and she were older this time.
S4.quote: It was people, but it was people choosing the machine.
S4.fieldNote: Her quiet acceptance runs out here. She has seen the picking robot with her own eyes and won't learn it. When I named the contradiction about the post office, she resolved it in one clear line. She'd understand Gareth's choice and still be sad, which is very her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, the last one. What would help is time. If they gave us five years' warning and let people like me finish out to retirement before the machines came in, I'd be content. And help to find work with people, because that's what I'm good at.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm happy. I am, mostly. I didn't expect to be, out in the rain at fifty-eight, but I am.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You're welcome. Mind the frost on the way out, the yard's like glass.

headlineQuote: A machine took my post office. I'd hate for one to take the pears as well, just when the trees have started to trust me.
portrait: Hana is a 58-year-old orchard worker who spent thirty years running a village post office counter before it closed. She doesn't use AI, keeps to the middle on politics, and handles change by quietly accepting it rather than fighting. In the office scenarios her worry is all for her daughter at a bank's head office. When robots reach the orchard, which she believes they would first, she says she won't learn them and would look for work with people instead.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because she's seen a picking robot and thinks orchards would be first.
whatWouldHelp: Time: several years' warning so people near retirement can finish out, and help finding work with people.
